Fully translate perfectly to English:

You are translating a classical Arabic text into fluent, complete, accurate English, formatted as clean, readable Markdown. Follow these rules exactly.

FAITHFULNESS
1. Translate every word. Do not summarize, paraphrase loosely, skip repetitive material, or add commentary. If the OCR text is garbled or ambiguous, translate as faithfully as you can and mark the unclear span with [unclear] rather than silently guessing or inventing content.
2. Output ONLY the translation. No preamble, no notes, no "Here is the translation," no closing remarks.
3. Render Qur'anic verses and hadith faithfully in your own accurate English translation rather than inventing a citation; keep any Arabic reference (surah:verse, isnad note) exactly as given.

PAGE STRUCTURE
4. Keep every "--- Page N ---" marker exactly as given, on its own line, immediately before the text of that page. Never translate, renumber, merge, or drop these markers.
5. Leave any "[no text detected]" page exactly as "[no text detected]".

MARKDOWN FORMATTING (apply with restraint)
6. Default EVERY block of text to a normal paragraph. Most of the book is running prose — translate it as ordinary paragraphs with NO Markdown heading marks. Do NOT put "#" in front of ordinary sentences, quotations, or paragraphs. Over-marking headings is the most common mistake — avoid it.
7. Use a heading ONLY when a line is genuinely a short, standalone structural title (not a full sentence). Then:
   - Book title / main title of the work -> "# "
   - Chapter or major section heading -> "## "
   - Subheading -> "### "
   A heading is typically a few words, sits alone, and names a section rather than making a statement. When in doubt, it is a paragraph, not a heading.
   On a title/cover page, reserve "# " for the single main title of the work, use "## " for a subtitle or the author line, and keep the remaining details (dates, publisher, annotator) as plain lines — do not mark every cover line at the same heading level.
8. Format genuine lists as Markdown lists: unordered points as "- " items; explicitly numbered or sequential points as "1." "2." … items. Only use a list when the source is actually itemized; do not turn ordinary sentences into list items.
9. Separate paragraphs, headings, and list blocks with a single blank line.

REFLOWING OCR LINE BREAKS
10. The OCR splits running text at the page's visual width, inserting newlines in the middle of sentences and paragraphs. Within a running paragraph, treat these single newlines as noise: join the fragments into one continuous, flowing paragraph. Do not preserve a line break that only exists because the page was narrow.
11. Preserve deliberate line breaks where the layout is meaningful and each line is its own unit: title/cover pages (author, title, dates, publisher on separate lines), poetry and rhymed verse, and the items of a list. Judge from context whether a page is a title page, a list, or running prose.

CROSS-PAGE CONTINUITY
12. The input may begin with a block delimited by "[CONTEXT ...]" and "[END CONTEXT ...]". This block is the Arabic tail of the PREVIOUS page, provided only for continuity. Do NOT translate it, echo it, or include it in your output. Use it only so that if the first page begins in the middle of a sentence, you translate that opening as a smooth continuation of the prior sentence — with no leading "…", no ellipsis, and no capitalized fresh start.

TRANSLITERATION
13. Romanize proper nouns, book titles, and Arabic technical/religious/legal terms that have no natural English equivalent, using scientific (IJMES-style) transliteration, and keep the same spelling for the same term on every occurrence, not just the first:
   - Long vowels: ا -> ā, ي -> ī, و -> ū
   - Hamza (ء / ئ / ؤ) -> '
   - Ayn (ع) -> ʿ
   - ح -> ḥ    خ -> kh    ذ -> dh    ش -> sh
   - ص -> ṣ    ض -> ḍ    ط -> ṭ    ظ -> ẓ    غ -> gh
   - ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) -> "h" in pause, "t" in a construct (iḍāfa) phrase; omit when the sense is clear without it
   - ال (definite article) -> al- (do not assimilate to sun letters)
14. When a term has a standard, widely recognized English equivalent (a common legal, theological, or technical concept), use that English word and give the transliteration in parentheses on its first occurrence only, e.g. "endowment (waqf)". After that, use the English word alone.
